title: Sprain
path: Management of Clients with Musculoskeletal Problems

headings.title: Introduction and Definition of a Sprain
headings.content: A **sprain** is an acute musculoskeletal injury involving the stretching or tearing of **ligaments**, which are the fibrous bands of connective tissue that connect bone to bone and stabilize joints. Unlike strains, which affect muscles or tendons, sprains strictly target joint capsules and supporting ligaments. The ankle, wrist, and knee are the most frequently affected sites, with the lateral ankle ligaments bearing the highest incidence globally. In busy Nigerian emergency and general outpatient departments, ankle sprains often occur due to uneven road surfaces, potholes, or poorly structured footwear during daily commuting.

headings.title: Pathophysiology and Grades of Sprains
headings.content:
When a joint is forced beyond its normal anatomical range of motion, microscopic tearing or complete rupture of the ligament fibers occurs. Tissue damage triggers an acute inflammatory response, characterized by vasodilation, capillary leakage, and localized edema. Clinically, sprains are classified into three distinct grades:

- **Grade I (Mild)**: Microscopic tearing of the ligament fibers; joint stability remains intact with minimal swelling and localized tenderness.
- **Grade II (Moderate)**: Partial macroscopic tear of the ligament; presents with moderate joint instability, significant swelling, bruising, and painful range of motion.
- **Grade III (Severe)**: Complete rupture of the ligament; results in gross joint instability, severe pain, extensive hematoma formation, and inability to bear weight.

headings.title: Clinical Manifestations and Assessment
headings.content: The clinical presentation of a sprain varies based on severity, but classic signs include localized pain, swelling, ecchymosis (bruising), and functional impairment. Assessment begins with a thorough health history detailing the mechanism of injury, such as a sudden twisting motion or an awkward landing. During physical examination, the nurse or clinician inspects for asymmetry and discoloration, palpates gently to identify focal points of maximal tenderness, and evaluates active and passive range of motion. Joint laxity tests are performed cautiously to determine structural stability without exacerbating tissue damage.

headings.title: Diagnostic Evaluation and Imaging
headings.content: While clinical history and physical examination provide the foundation for diagnosis, imaging studies are frequently necessary to rule out associated bony fractures. Plain radiography, or X-rays, is the initial imaging modality of choice, often guided by standardized clinical decision rules like the Ottawa Ankle Rules to avoid unnecessary radiation. When soft tissue damage is extensive, or if chronic instability persists despite conservative treatment, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is utilized to visualize detailed ligamentous, meniscal, and cartilaginous architecture.

headings.title: Medical Management and Surgical Interventions
headings.content: Management strategies depend directly on the grade of the sprain. Grade I and II sprains are primarily managed conservatively with activity modification, short-term immobilization using braces or splints, and pharmacological pain management using non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) or analgesics. Grade III sprains, particularly in young, athletic individuals or those involving high-stress joints like the knee, may require orthopedic surgical consultation for arthroscopic repair or ligament reconstruction to restore long-term stability.

headings.title: Nursing Interventions and the RICE Protocol
headings.content:
Immediate nursing care for acute sprains centers on the classic **RICE** protocol to limit secondary tissue damage and control inflammation:

- **Rest**: Prevent further stress on the injured ligament by discontinuing weight-bearing activities.
- **Ice**: Apply cold packs intermittently (15 to 20 minutes at a time) to induce vasoconstriction and reduce swelling and pain.
- **Compression**: Use an elastic bandage wrapped distally to proximally to minimize interstitial fluid accumulation.
- **Elevation**: Raise the injured extremity above the level of the heart to promote venous and lymphatic return against gravity.

headings.title: Rehabilitation and Physiotherapy
headings.content: Once the acute inflammatory phase subsides, structured rehabilitation is vital to restore full function and prevent chronic joint instability. Physiotherapy begins with gentle passive range-of-motion exercises, progressing gradually to active movement and strengthening exercises targeting the muscles surrounding the joint. Proprioceptive and balance training are integrated later in the recovery phase to retrain neuromuscular pathways, reducing the high risk of recurrent sprains in patients returning to work, sports, or daily activities.

headings.title: Complications and Prevention Strategies
headings.content: Inadequate healing or premature return to high-impact activities can lead to long-term complications, notably **chronic joint instability**, persistent pain, post-traumatic stiffness, and recurrent sprains. Preventative nursing education focuses on teaching proper footwear selection, ankle-strengthening exercises for high-risk individuals, and environmental safety awareness. Emphasizing the completion of full rehabilitation programs ensures that surrounding musculature provides adequate dynamic support to compensate for lax or repaired ligaments.
